slide.title: Automate, Support or Enable?
slide.body: Three columns with icons: gears (Automate) · person with chart (Support) · spark (Enable). Small tag: AI Literacy for Leaders · Lesson 2.

scenes.voiceover: Many organisations start with one question. Where can we use AI? A better question is this. Which of our tasks cost the most time, create the most errors or slow down our customers? Value comes from the task, not from the technology.

slide.title: Where AI Creates Value
slide.body: AI Literacy for Leaders and Executives · Lesson 2 of 10

scenes.voiceover: In the last lesson, we learned the five terms leaders need. Now let's ask where AI actually creates value. In most organisations, it does so in three ways.

slide.title: 1. Automate routine tasks
slide.body: Repetitive · high volume · low judgement. Examples: sorting documents, extracting form data, routing requests. Value: time saved, fewer errors. People handle exceptions.

scenes.voiceover: The first way is automating routine tasks. This is work that is repetitive, high in volume and low in judgement, such as sorting documents or routing requests. The value is saved time and fewer manual errors. People stay responsible for the exceptions.

slide.title: 2. Support decisions
slide.body: AI informs, the person decides. Examples: flag unusual transactions, forecast demand, summarise reports. Often the safest place to start.

scenes.voiceover: The second way is supporting people's decisions. AI gives a person better information, but the person still decides. Think of flagging unusual transactions or forecasting demand. This is often the safest place to start, because a human checks every important outcome.

slide.title: 3. Enable new products
slide.body: Something not practical before: a 24-hour service, advice tailored to each customer. Value: growth, new reach. Highest uncertainty.

scenes.voiceover: The third way is enabling new products or services, such as a service available at any hour. The value is growth or new reach. But it is also the most uncertain, because it depends on customers accepting something new.

slide.title: Four features of a good AI task
slide.body: Four ticked boxes: Frequent · Patterned · Has data · Mistakes can be caught. Below, a red box: Rare, high-trust or severe single errors → strong human control or not suitable.

scenes.voiceover: A good task for AI has four features. It happens often. It follows a pattern. There is data about it. And a mistake can be caught and corrected. A rare task, or one where a single error is severe, usually needs strong human control, or no AI at all.

slide.title: Value has a price
slide.body: Scale: left pan 'Benefit', right pan 'Data + People + Workflow change + Ongoing cost'. Caption: value only if benefit is larger.

scenes.voiceover: Value also has a price. Every use case needs data, people who can use and check it, changes to the workflow and ongoing cost. We cover these costs in the next lesson. For now, remember this. A use case only creates value if the benefit is larger than all of those costs together.

scenes.stock_query: manager interviewing new team member office
scenes.voiceover: Here is a useful way to think about it. AI is like a new team member with a very specific skill set. You would not hire a person and then look for work to give them. You find the work first, then choose who fits. AI should be chosen the same way.

scenes.stock_query: logistics office staff processing delivery paperwork
scenes.voiceover: Let's look at three fictional organisations, one for each type of value. First, automate. Katarzyna Nowak runs operations at a freight company in Poland. Her team types details from hundreds of scanned delivery notes every day.

slide.title: Automate: delivery notes
slide.body: Scanned notes → AI reads and fills system → uncertain notes go to staff. Side tag: Control = daily sample check.

scenes.voiceover: An AI document tool now reads the notes and fills in the system. Staff check only the notes the tool marks as uncertain. The value is time saved and fewer typing errors, and the control is a daily sample check.

scenes.stock_query: hospital administrators planning staff schedule together
scenes.voiceover: Second, support. Wanjiru Kamau leads administration at a public hospital in Kenya. A forecasting tool uses past patient arrival records to predict busy days one week ahead. Her team still builds the staff rota, but with better information. Patient data stays inside the hospital's approved systems.

scenes.stock_query: customer using banking chat on phone evening
scenes.voiceover: Third, enable. Rafael Souza is head of digital services at a regional bank in Brazil. The bank adds a chat assistant that answers simple questions in Portuguese at any hour. This is a new service, not only a faster old one. Rafael limits it to general questions, and hands anything about a customer's account to a human.

slide.title: Control matches risk
slide.body: Three rows: Poland, Automate → daily sample check. Kenya, Support → people build the rota. Brazil, Enable → general questions only, hand-off to a human. Footer: Start with tasks you know well.

scenes.voiceover: Notice that each leader chose the level of AI control based on the risk of a mistake, not on what the technology could do. And avoid a common mistake. New products sound strategic, but most organisations get faster, safer results by first automating or supporting tasks they already know well.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Three ways: automate · support · enable. 2. Good tasks: frequent, patterned, have data, errors can be caught. 3. Start from the problem, not the technology.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, AI creates value in three main ways: automating routine tasks, supporting decisions and enabling new products or services. Second, good tasks for AI happen often, follow a pattern, have data and allow mistakes to be caught. Third, start from the problem and its cost, not from the technology.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will list ten tasks your team does every week. You will label each one automate, support or not suitable for AI, with a one-line reason. In the next lesson, we look at the real costs of AI: data, people and process. See you there.
